inserts.title: Head filtering adds a horizontal level cue
paragraphs: The head-related transfer function describes how the head and external ears change the level and phase of each frequency arriving from a particular direction. Measuring it close to the eardrum captures the filtering that the animal actually receives. The facial ruff and the asymmetric ears contribute to this filtering, which shapes both cues before any neuron responds to them.

Acoustic measurements and playback tests used directions corresponding to interaural delays of 50, 100, and 150 µs. Natural level cues reduced the timing ambiguities present at these delays. A timing value alone can match more than one direction, so the level cue helps choose among the candidates. The playback tests kept the level cues natural for each direction.

The ILD also carries an azimuthal component, which the frontal measurements show beside its strong dependence on elevation. A small horizontal component of the level cue can matter when timing admits two competing locations, and it can decide between them. Each direction fixes a pair of timing and level values that the owl can use together.
notes: Head filtering adds a horizontal level cue.

inserts.title: Earphones isolate one binaural cue
paragraphs: Earphones allowed one binaural cue to change without the acoustically coupled changes that a moving real speaker produces. Holding the other cue fixed showed whether a preference shifted when the other input changed. Each series changed one cue while the other stayed fixed. The two cues were varied in separate series on the same neuron.

The key observation concerned the position of each tuning peak rather than whether every spike count stayed identical across conditions. Peak position, not identical spike counts, defined each preference. A shifted peak indicates a change in preference, while a change in spike count alone reflects a change in response magnitude. The same logic applied to each series.

Calibrated earphones delivered every condition, so the sound level reaching each ear was known. The peak positions can be read against a controlled acoustic setting. Each series varied a single cue in the same neuron. The same neuron was tested in every series, so the values are directly matched. Acoustic conditions stayed matched across series.
notes: Earphones isolate one binaural cue.

inserts.title: Parallel nuclei transform a shared input
paragraphs: Auditory-nerve fibers carry both temporal and level information. Parallel nuclei can emphasize different variables while receiving the same peripheral input, because each nucleus reads that shared signal in its own way. Neurons in each nucleus thus carry different features of the same sound. The nucleus determines which variable is kept in its output. Each nucleus thus has a distinct output.

The relevant difference lies in how each nucleus transforms its shared peripheral input, not in which signals reach it. The original micrograph supplies the positions of the nuclei and a scale bar for the sections. The labeled structures are experimental tissue from the study itself, not a schematic circuit. The labeled nuclei are shown at the scale of the sections.

Histological landmarks supplied the reference points for intracellular recording and tracer experiments. Each recording depth could then be assigned to a named nucleus before its responses were interpreted. Histology was thus the anatomical basis for the later measurements. The landmarks were visible in each transverse section. Each named nucleus then carried its own recordings in that section.
notes: Parallel nuclei transform a shared input.

inserts.title: Calibrated tones define the phase measure
paragraphs: The study used ear-canal calibration for individual animals, so the stimulus level was measured at the auditory input rather than inferred from a speaker setting. Each level value is tied to the sound that actually reached that animal's ear. The calibrated value is the level at the auditory input, not at the speaker. Calibration is what makes the levels comparable across animals.

Vector strength pools phase values across many cycles of the tone. A high-frequency neuron can still carry information about its preferred stimulus phase while firing on a subset of cycles. Each cycle contributes its phase to the vector, so more cycles give a more stable estimate. The stimulus was a tone of fixed frequency and level.

Detectable locking is not equivalent to equally precise locking at every frequency. Phase locking should be read frequency by frequency, since the precision of the timing signal changes across the range. Phase organization can be measured at a sound level below the rate threshold. Its precision depends on frequency and level together. Its precision depends on frequency and level together.
notes: Calibrated tones define the phase measure.

inserts.title: Reconstructed arbors show layout, not length
paragraphs: The original authors reconstructed three-dimensional axon arbors across serial sections and then adjusted their projection onto the published two-dimensional view. The figure is cropped unchanged from the article, and its scale bar represents 1 mm. The figure thus shows a layout rather than a measurement. The scale bar sets the size of that layout in physical units.

The drawing's geometry shows the arrangement of the branches, not an exact flattened measurement of each branch length. Physical separation in the drawing is a guide to layout rather than a measured distance. Each branch in the drawing traces a path from NM to one border. Relative positions along each border can be read directly from the drawing.

The reconstruction is a published anatomical result, so its geometry comes from the authors' own tracing rather than from a schematic drawing. Readers can treat its layout as the authors' record of the labeled axons in those sections. Tracing shows where axons go, so it identifies the entry geometry that a delay line needs to work.

inserts.title: Myelin spacing is one anatomical contributor
paragraphs: Nodes are interruptions of the myelin sheath, and nodal spacing is one anatomical contributor to impulse propagation. The internodal measurements describe a structural feature that could affect conduction speed in these axons. Impulse propagation is renewed at each node, which keeps the signal moving along the fiber. The spacing of those nodes sets how often this renewal occurs along the axon.

The interpretation combines measured axonal anatomy with measured conduction delays. The mechanistic inference is kept separate from those measurements, so each claim stays tied to its own evidence. Conduction velocity estimates come from the physiology of the same preparation. Those estimates place delay generation within the range seen in these axons. Those values are local estimates rather than whole-axon measurements.

Both kinds of measurement were made in the same HRP-labeled axons, which links the spacing to the delay gradients. The anatomy and the physiology share one reference, the labeled fiber itself. The authors used those same labeled fibers for every measurement reported. Their combined reading supports the proposal in this single preparation. Those results support the proposal directly.
notes: Myelin spacing is one anatomical contributor.

inserts.title: Recorded peaks match across recording types
paragraphs: The curves are normalized to each recording's maximum, so alignment refers to relative response levels rather than identical absolute firing. Relative response levels are thus comparable across recordings. Absolute spike counts can differ between the recordings without changing the alignment. This normalization puts the peaks of different recordings on a common scale. Relative response levels are comparable across the recordings.

The study compared single-unit and multi-unit recordings and found closely matching peak positions. Those matching positions show that the array-specific delay appears in both kinds of recording. Single-unit recordings isolate one neuron, while multi-unit recordings sample a population of neurons. Both record the same delay, so the array's timing value is consistent across the two sampling methods.

A preferred phase for one frequency is insufficient to identify the array-specific ITD without the cross-frequency relation. The timing value emerges when the frequencies are considered together. Frequencies examined one at a time leave the array delay undetermined. Pooling across frequencies resolves that ambiguity in the array. A shared relation across frequencies gives a single timing value.

inserts.title: Injections label a restricted target region
paragraphs: An injection region can encompass more than one cell, so the result concerns a restricted target region rather than a complete single-cell wiring diagram. The synaptic weight of each labeled cell lies outside what this method measures. The labeled population is thus a region-level description of the projection. Retrograde labeling identifies a source region, not a single cell.

The experiment combines two independent kinds of evidence: physiological cue tuning and anatomical projection labeling. Each kind of evidence points to the same array-to-region link from a different direction. The matched timing preferences give the physiological side of the same projection. The link between ICC and ICx is thus shown from two directions in this preparation.

The published sections keep the labeled somata and the response curves together, so the anatomy and the physiology can be read side by side. The scale bars give the size of the labeled region in the tissue. Retrograde tracing shows where a projection starts, while the physiology shows what the labeled cells respond to in this study.

inserts.title: Convergence needs a level control
paragraphs: Two tones share a true imposed interaural delay, while their repeated phase matches occur at different delays. Their joint presentation favors the one delay that both channels agree on. The pair thus isolates the agreement between two frequency channels. Each tone alone produces its own set of repeated peaks. The shared delay is the one that survives the combination.

Component-only conditions isolate integration from a plain rise in sound energy. The joint response can then be attributed to agreement between channels rather than to added energy. The condition isolates the effect of combining channels, which is the quantity of interest. Its result is then set against the single-tone responses in the same cell.

Each tone's repeated maxima sit at different delays, so the pair can reveal the one delay the two channels share. The convergence mechanism is tested by this shared delay. The convergence mechanism predicts that agreement favors this delay. Other nonlinear steps can add to the selectivity in the same cell. The published analysis compares the response to that expectation directly.
notes: Convergence needs a level control.

The authors grouped cells by their relative position within each penetration. The ordering reflects a physiological-anatomical relation, not a measurement of external elevation in degrees. Each penetration thus provides its own ordered sequence of sites. Cells were ordered within each penetration. Those sequences were examined for a dorsal-to-ventral trend, which was consistent across all the penetrations sampled.

This organization is internal to VLVp and describes the level-threshold axis of that nucleus, not space itself. Later stages of the pathway can read these graded values directly. The graded values sit on an axis that ranges from contralateral to ipsilateral bias. That axis, not a spatial coordinate, organizes the nucleus. This ordering gives a graded map of thresholds in the level pathway.

inserts.title: Remote inhibition reverses within an hour
paragraphs: Disinhibition means that activity increases after an inhibitory influence is removed. A drug that blocks GABA-A receptors can raise the output of a population instead of exciting it directly. GABA-A receptors carry that inhibition in this case. Blocking them lifts that inhibition from the target population. The projection then carries more activity to its targets.

The sign of a drug's effect at the injection site can differ from the sign of its effect at a distant recording site. Injection spread and network effects make it hard to assign the whole effect to one synapse. The distant recording site was in the lateral shell. Its response was tracked over time. Responses were tracked over several minutes after injection.

Reversible changes and the time course of recovery help distinguish acute circuit modulation from irreversible tissue damage. The lateral-shell recovery in this study points to modulation rather than injury. The time course of recovery in the study ran for about an hour. That timescale fits a change in circuit activity more than a lesion. Recovery began within the study's observation period.
notes: Remote inhibition reverses within an hour.

The surrounding inhibitory regions were retained in the authors' maps, so suppression outside the excitatory field is part of each map. Those inhibitory zones shape where the edges of the field fall. The authors' maps thus include that suppressive surround. The maps record both excitation and suppression. The retained regions shape how far suppression extends across the field.

inserts.title: Membrane products multiply timing and level
paragraphs: An analog conjunction can permit firing when both timing and level are favorable. The fitted multiplicative term describes membrane responses in which neither cue alone produces a strong response. Such a conjunction is a multiplication of the two cue effects. In this account, the response is strongest where both cue effects are large. In that case the response depends on both cues at once.

The analysis leaves open whether a particular receptor or dendritic compartment performs the multiplication itself. The fit describes the membrane response, not the molecular mechanism that produces it. The fitted term is a mathematical description of a physiological response. The matrix of membrane responses forms the basis of the fit. This mathematical form is the authors' central analytical step.

Smaller contributions from other interactions remain possible alongside the multiplicative component. The published analysis reports the dominant structure of the matrix rather than an exhaustive decomposition. The studied neurons were ICx cells recorded intracellularly. The fit accounts for most of the structure in those matrices. Those matrices were built from subthreshold recordings in each neuron.
notes: Membrane products multiply timing and level.

inserts.title: GABA-A blockade broadens timing tuning
paragraphs: The half-peak width measures the range of delays over which a response remains above half of its peak. A broader curve indicates weaker selectivity even if the maximum response rises. The width is a separate measure from the height of the peak. Peak height and width thus measure different aspects of tuning. The authors reported both measures for each curve.

Applying GABA produced effects opposite to those of BMI in the same tissue. This reversal is the pattern expected if GABA-A receptors mediate the inhibition. The opposite effects point to GABA-A receptors rather than to a general effect of drug delivery. The reverse pattern is the key evidence in this analysis. BMI and GABA act on the same receptor family.

Simultaneous BMI could antagonize those GABA effects, which supports a GABA-receptor-mediated interpretation of the result. Recovery after the drug confirmed that the effect was reversible in each cell. The cells were recorded before, during, and after drug application. The timing curves were compared across those three intervals. Each interval produced its own measured tuning width.

2: The **barn owl**, Tyto alba, is a nocturnal predator whose auditory system converts the sounds made by prey into directed head movements. Azimuth describes horizontal direction and elevation describes vertical direction. Because head turns can be recorded directly, they give a behavioral measure of the location the owl perceives, even without visual guidance from the prey.

Kettler and colleagues recorded head orientation while sounds were presented through earphones, which gave direct control over the acoustic difference between the two ears. With an interaural delay of 100 µs, broadband noise produced turns toward the corresponding target. A 5-kHz tone could instead elicit turns toward an alternative location in the opposite hemifield.

This **phantom source** is a localization illusion rather than a second physical loudspeaker. Broadband and 1.5-kHz-wide narrowband stimuli separated spectral effects from changes in the imposed delay. The behavior therefore links auditory timing ambiguity to an observable orienting decision that the experimenters could measure in the same birds. Both stimulus types were presented to the same birds.
3: **Interaural time difference**, or ITD, is the difference in sound arrival time between the ears, measured in microseconds. **Interaural level difference**, or ILD, is the difference in sound pressure level, measured in decibels. Neither cue is a location label when it first reaches the auditory nerve, so the brain must derive direction from the two cues together.

Kettler and colleagues used ear-canal probe microphones to measure how the head filters sound before it reaches the eardrum. The frontal ITD map varied chiefly with azimuth, while ILD varied strongly with elevation. Each cue therefore carries information about a different axis of the sound's location in space. These measurements cover every frontal direction.

The familiar pairing of ITD with horizontal direction and ILD with vertical direction is a useful specialization. It describes the dominant relation in these measurements. The two cues therefore carry complementary information, and the owl's auditory system uses both to build a single estimate of where the sound originates. This two-cue arrangement is central to how the owl localizes sound.
4: A **receptive field** is the set of stimulus conditions that changes a neuron's activity. Knudsen and Konishi mapped auditory receptive fields by moving a loudspeaker around the head of a lightly anesthetized owl in an anechoic chamber, which minimized reflected sound. Extracellular electrodes recorded the spikes of each unit at every speaker position.

Noise bursts lasted 100 ms and were delivered 10 dB above each unit's threshold while speaker positions were sampled in azimuth and elevation. The **best area** is defined by the positions that produce maximal responses rather than merely detectable ones. Its center lies at the most effective stimulus position for that neuron.

Most mapped fields were vertically elongated. Their widths ranged from 7° to 40° in azimuth, with a mean of 25°. A broad response boundary and a smaller best area describe different aspects of selectivity, so neither one alone gives the owl's threshold for localizing a sound. Each field is therefore a region of space rather than a single point.
5: Knudsen and Konishi reconstructed electrode tracks histologically and compared each recording position with the center of the neuron's best area. The auditory region is **MLD**, nucleus mesencephalicus lateralis dorsalis, the avian homolog of the inferior colliculus. The reconstructed tracks tied each recording to a specific location in the tissue. Histology supplied the anatomical reference for the map.

Best-area azimuth shifted from about 60° contralateral in the posterolateral region to 15° ipsilateral in the anteromedial region. Best-area elevation ranged from about +20° to −90°, and neighboring neurons generally had overlapping receptive fields. Adjacent neurons therefore represent adjacent sound locations. Each recording site contributes one point to the spatial order of the map.

Tone bursts, clicks, and noise usually preserved the best-area location, and changing the level from 10 to 30 dB above threshold also left it in place. This stability supports a **computed map of auditory space** rather than a simple map of frequency or loudness. The result holds across all three sound types tested.
6: A **tuning curve** relates a neuron's response to a controlled stimulus parameter. Takahashi, Moiseff, and Konishi varied ITD while holding ILD fixed, then varied ILD while holding ITD fixed, recording from space-specific midbrain neurons. Each curve therefore isolates one binaural cue at a time. The two cues were tested one at a time.

The timing-sensitive tuning in each nucleus responded differently to that same drug, which shows that the effect is specific to each nucleus.

GABAergic inhibition therefore sharpens the timing representation at selected collicular stages rather than creating timing sensitivity everywhere. The antagonist result identifies a receptor-sensitive contribution to this sharpening. The sharpened curve is the measurable outcome of that receptor action. Inhibition sets the width of each curve. Recovery after drug application confirmed the reversibility.
43: Fujita and Konishi compared broadband ICx timing responses before and during local GABA-A receptor blockade. Broadband input normally emphasizes a principal timing peak while suppressing the repeated matches inherited from narrowband channels. The same ICx neurons were tested under both conditions. The contrast was tested within the same neuron under each condition.

BMI increased the secondary-peak responses and restored phase ambiguity for noise. Records show time-dependent increases at delays such as −270 and +120 µs, while the principal timing preference remained distinguishable from the new peaks. Recovery measurements tested reversibility after drug application. Secondary-to-primary relations were analyzed alongside the time courses in each recording.

Cross-frequency convergence and inhibitory suppression support **unique broadband timing selectivity**. Inhibition is one of two mechanisms that keep the principal delay dominant in the ICx output. Convergence supplies agreement across frequencies, and inhibition removes the competing matches that remain in each neuron. The main peak thus stays on top of the others.
44: **Glutamate** is an excitatory transmitter. Feldman and Knudsen applied AP5, an antagonist of NMDA receptors, and CNQX, a non-NMDA glutamate-receptor antagonist, by iontophoresis while recording from ICx and the ICC lateral shell. Iontophoresis uses an electrical current to deliver each drug locally. Each antagonist was tested alone and in combination in each preparation.

AP5 removed about 55% of auditory-evoked spikes at ICx multiunit sites and 64% at single units. In the lateral shell, the corresponding reductions were about 19% and 25%, and combined AP5 and CNQX strongly suppressed responses in both subdivisions. The combined antagonist condition tested whether a weak AP5 effect reflected little NMDA contribution.

**NMDA-dependent transmission** contributes more to ICx responses, while non-NMDA transmission is substantial in both regions. Spike reduction measures functional contribution rather than receptor abundance at the synapse. The contrast between NMDA and non-NMDA components therefore differs by region. The ICx responses depend more heavily on NMDA transmission than the lateral shell does.
45: Feldman and Knudsen analyzed **peristimulus time histograms**, which align repeated spike trains to sound onset. They tested ICx units with transient, sustained, or mixed responses to 50-ms broadband stimuli at each unit's preferred ITD and ILD. Each unit was classified by its response type before the drug was applied in each unit

AP5 at 25 nA reduced spikes, with a larger effect on late activity in mixed transient-sustained responses. CNQX, by contrast, reduced activity more uniformly across the response time course. The reduction was measured before, during, and after application in each unit. Responses were measured in each unit before, during, and after the drug.

The temporal difference fits slower NMDA-dependent excitation supplementing faster non-NMDA transmission. Together with coincidence detection, bilateral inhibition, and cross-frequency convergence, this synaptic integration supports the sustained spatial signals available for owl orienting. The late component of the ICx response builds up over the stimulus duration. This slow excitation adds to the response across long stimuli.
